Six minds. One shared mission.

We are Celestial Six, a six-member team from Karachi with interests in AI, data science, software development, and design. We aim to turn NASA’s open data into practical solutions to real-world challenges, combining thoughtful research, creative ideas, and clear storytelling.

Our team is already formed. Join requests are open only for our five existing teammates to complete their registration.
summary:
Burning Calendar transforms over 25 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire observations into an interactive burning-activity calendar for Pakistan. MODIS and VIIRS detect hotspots at different spatial resolutions, making raw counts unsuitable for direct long-term comparison. Our Python pipeline cleans and harmonizes their records by learning month-specific VIIRS-to-MODIS scaling factors from overlapping years, applying those factors to earlier MODIS counts, and estimating uncertainty.

In leave-one-year-out validation across 2013–2025, this method achieved an R² of 0.908 and a 14.1% weighted absolute percentage error for monthly counts, compared with an R² of 0.728 for a single-factor baseline.

Built with Streamlit, the application offers monthly and daily calendars, user-defined geographic areas, anomaly and trend analysis, hotspot maps, downloadable results, and an optional near-real-time NASA FIRMS view.

Burning Calendar makes long-term satellite observations more consistent and accessible for researchers, environmental planners, and other users studying patterns and unusual periods of burning activity.
details:
Burning Calendar — Project Details

The Problem

Satellite-based fire monitoring provides valuable information about wildfires, agricultural burning, and other thermal activity. However, historical fire records are difficult to compare consistently because different satellite instruments detect hotspots at different spatial resolutions and sensitivities.

NASA's MODIS instruments, aboard the Terra and Aqua satellites, provide observations dating back to 2000 at approximately 1 km resolution. VIIRS provides higher-resolution observations at 375 m, allowing it to detect smaller hotspots that MODIS may miss.

As a result, an apparent increase in hotspot counts over time may reflect changes in satellite detection capability rather than actual changes in burning activity.

Burning Calendar addresses this challenge by harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS observations into a consistent time series and presenting the results through an interactive web application.

Our Solution

We developed a Python-based satellite data processing pipeline and a Streamlit web application that transforms NASA FIRMS active-fire observations into an accessible burning activity calendar.

The current implementation focuses on Pakistan, using satellite observations from November 2000 through October 2026.

Our system processes historical MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m observations, combines them into a standardized analytical dataset, and enables users to investigate burning activity across different geographical areas and time periods.

The application goes beyond displaying raw hotspot counts by introducing sensor harmonization, uncertainty estimation, historical anomaly detection, seasonal analysis, and statistical trend evaluation.

Methodology and Technical Implementation

1. Data Collection and Preprocessing

We obtained historical and near-real-time MODIS and VIIRS datasets through NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS).

Our data preparation pipeline removes duplicate records, filters low-confidence detections, and excludes non-vegetation fire classifications where the relevant attribute is available.

After preprocessing, our Pakistan dataset contains 926,921 cleaned satellite detections, including 228,601 MODIS and 698,320 VIIRS observations.

2. MODIS–VIIRS Harmonization

To address differences in satellite detection sensitivity, we developed a month-specific calibration approach.

During the years when MODIS and VIIRS observations overlap, the system calculates the ratio of VIIRS to MODIS hotspot detections for each calendar month.

These factors are subsequently applied to historical MODIS counts recorded before the VIIRS period, converting them into estimated VIIRS-equivalent hotspot counts.

For the Pakistan dataset, the overall VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio is approximately 4.55, while monthly calibration factors range from approximately 3.17 to 8.39. This demonstrates why using a single correction factor throughout the year can be misleading.

The resulting harmonized dataset contains 312 monthly observations, extending from November 2000 through October 2026.

3. Regional Calibration and Uncertainty Estimation

When users select a geographical area, the application recalculates the harmonization factors using observations from that region.

If insufficient observations are available for reliable local calibration, the system falls back to the broader regional factors.

We also estimate the uncertainty associated with historical scaling through the 10th and 90th percentiles of annual calibration-factor variation. These ranges help users interpret historical estimates responsibly rather than treating them as exact measurements.

4. Statistical Validation

We evaluated our harmonization method using leave-one-year-out cross-validation across 13 overlapping years, from 2013 to 2025.

In each evaluation, one year's observations were excluded from calibration, and MODIS-based estimates were compared against the corresponding observed VIIRS counts.

Our month-specific approach achieved:

  • R² of 0.908
  • Weighted Absolute Percentage Error of 14.1%
  • Overall bias of approximately +0.4%

A simpler single-factor approach achieved an R² of 0.728 and a weighted absolute percentage error of 28.3%.

These results demonstrate substantially improved monthly agreement when seasonal differences between satellite instruments are considered. Annual-total errors were similar for the two methods, so the main measured improvement is in monthly consistency.

Implemented Web Application Features

We created a multi-tab interactive dashboard offering the following functionality:

Burning Activity Calendar: Displays monthly and daily hotspot activity across the historical record. Users can view counts, deviations from historical averages, and five descriptive activity categories ranging from much below normal to much above normal.

Historical Year Comparison: Allows users to compare the cumulative hotspot activity of a selected year with the typical historical range, making unusually active or inactive periods easier to identify.

Trend and Seasonal Analysis: Uses Sen's slope and the Mann-Kendall statistical test to evaluate long-term changes in hotspot activity. The application also identifies the months representing the typical fire season and visualizes changes in peak burning months across years.

Interactive Geographical Mapping: Displays the spatial distribution and density of satellite hotspots. Users can examine the entire region, draw a polygon on a map, specify geographical boundaries, or select a location using coordinates and a search radius.

Near-Real-Time Monitoring: Includes an optional NASA FIRMS API integration for retrieving recent VIIRS NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 observations. With a valid API key, users can compare recent hotspot counts against equivalent calendar dates in previous years.

Transparent Methodology: Provides access to explanations of the harmonization process, calibration factors, uncertainty estimates, and validation results.

Data Export: Allows users to download filtered hotspot observations, harmonized monthly statistics, scaling factors, and analytical summaries for further investigation.

Technologies and Development Tools

Our application was developed using Python and Streamlit, supported by:

  • pandas and NumPy: Satellite data processing, filtering, and numerical calculations.
  • Altair: Interactive charts, calendars, and statistical visualizations.
  • Folium, streamlit-folium, and pydeck: Geographical exploration, custom area selection, and hotspot mapping.
  • PyArrow and Parquet: Efficient storage and retrieval of processed satellite observations.
  • Requests: Communication with NASA's FIRMS API.
  • pytest: Automated testing of data processing, harmonization, geographical filtering, and API-related functionality.

The application follows a modular software structure, separating data processing, sensor harmonization, analytical calculations, geographical operations, live-data retrieval, and user-interface styling.

Creativity and Innovation

Burning Calendar's primary innovation lies in combining transparent satellite-data harmonization with an intuitive visual exploration experience.

Instead of directly combining incompatible sensor counts or relying on a single scaling factor, our system accounts for seasonal differences, adapts calibration to selected geographical regions, and provides uncertainty estimates supported by cross-validation.

It also transforms complex analytical outputs into understandable calendars, historical comparisons, and descriptive activity classifications.

A customized sunset-inspired interface, interactive geographic selection, and integrated data downloads make the platform approachable for users with varying levels of technical expertise.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Burning Calendar is designed to help environmental researchers, land managers, agricultural planners, educators, and fire-monitoring organizations better understand historical burning patterns.

By making long-term satellite observations easier to compare and interpret, the application supports the identification of seasonal burning periods, unusual activity, geographical concentrations of hotspots, and long-term changes in observed burning activity.

Our implementation using Pakistan demonstrates how NASA Earth observation resources can be transformed into accessible environmental information, with the potential to extend the approach to additional geographical regions.

Challenges, Limitations, and Future Scope

The primary technical challenge addressed by our system is the difference in MODIS and VIIRS detection characteristics. Our solution uses seasonal calibration, local adjustments, and validation to reduce the resulting inconsistencies.

We also considered data quality, sensor uncertainty, geographical filtering, accessibility, API integration, and efficient processing of large historical datasets.

It is important to recognize that a satellite hotspot does not necessarily represent one individual fire. Clouds, smoke, satellite viewing conditions, and sensor sensitivity can affect detection counts. Historical VIIRS-equivalent values are statistical estimates, not direct observations.

The near-real-time functionality depends on NASA FIRMS API access and the continued availability of the relevant satellite products.

Future development could include expanding geographical coverage, additional cross-sensor calibration, automated dataset updates, and fire radiative power analysis for a richer understanding of burning intensity.

Conclusion

Burning Calendar demonstrates how NASA's long-term Earth observation data can be transformed into a harmonized, interpretable, and interactive environmental monitoring resource.

By combining satellite data processing, statistical validation, regional exploration, and accessible visualizations, our project offers a practical approach to understanding when and where burning activity occurs and how it compares with historical conditions.
